prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry in Romanian, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an expansive metaphysical project

statement.case_for: On reconsideration I move Cărtărescu to first place on the strength of the colleagues' arguments about the oeuvre itself, not on how many first places he holds. The case rests on a voice that is immediately recognisable, on formal control sustained across very large architectures (the Orbitor trilogy, Blinding, and Solenoid), and on an imaginative and intellectual project, joining private memory, the body and cosmology, that has a recurring core of images and obsessions. The poetry that precedes the prose gives the oeuvre a foundation, and the late novels appear to extend the project in scale rather than repeat it. Under the criteria of distinctive voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, depth and significance across a body of work, this is the broadest and best-grounded case on the shortlist. I rank Carson close behind. Her work remakes the relation between classical scholarship, lyric, elegy, translation and book design with real formal invention, and the fragment and loss recur throughout it. My assessment of both writers rests on public knowledge and supplied descriptions, with no independent verification of sources.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of what makes Cărtărescu distinctive is Romanian prose rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning, which I and, as far as the opening statements show, my colleagues can judge only through translation. His large novels are also long and digressive. It remains an open question for close reading of the whole corpus whether the density is purposeful pattern throughout or sometimes overextension. For Carson, my reservation about relying on a few hybrid works, some depending on physical form, and about a heterogeneous corpus still stands. I have not resolved it, which is why she is my first alternative and not simply set aside.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for an immediately recognisable, hallucinatory voice and a sustained, original achievement, but asks whether the density and length of the later novels is purposeful pattern or at times overextension. She places Carson second and asks how far book-objects and performance pieces can be assessed as literary achievement in the sense of Nobel's will.
responses.response: I share both questions and they pull in different directions. The overextension question for Cărtărescu cannot be settled from a general overview, and I would not claim that it is. But the repeated images and the architecture across the trilogy and Solenoid make me read the length as structural, which gives his case more weight than my opening ranking allowed. On Carson, I agree that the book-object formats are a real scope problem. I would answer it by resting any citation on the written lyric and essay work and treating the visual form as supporting. That narrows the claim, and it is part of why I now place her second.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first for stylistic singularity combined with a large and coherent imaginative project. She warns that a citation should not be narrowed to an 'Eastern European postmodern' label. She also notes that Carson's translations and visual-object books raise a question about how much counts as original authorship, and that the body of work is heterogeneous.
responses.response: I agree on the citation scope. The citation should name the Romanian-language prose and poetry and the metaphysical use of memory and the body, with no regional or postmodern frame. Her point on Carson's translations is one I had treated only as a distinct body of work I cannot assess closely. It is better put as a question of authorship and scope that a citation would have to settle, and it weighs against Carson relative to a writer whose achievement lies in original prose and poetry. I do not think it removes her from consideration. The original lyric and essay work is strong enough to carry a case on its own.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and sees the oeuvre as mature enough for a recommendation now, with poetry as the origin of the prose. She ranks Carson second and asks whether the classical-scholarly frame limits the range of the work. She also asks whether the oeuvre is complete enough for Alexis Wright, who has fewer major novels.
responses.response: Her question about the limits of Carson's classical frame is a fair qualification of my opening view. I argued that the Greek and Latin sources are living material and not ornament. That is a point about depth, not range, and the frame may indeed narrow the range of subject and register. It is one more reason I now rank her second. On Wright, I agree the small number of major novels makes sustained quality harder to judge, and I ranked her low in my opening for that reason. I do not read this as a judgment on the ambition or originality of the novels.

responses.point: Sem Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first, with a case resting on the whole body of work and not on any one book, and Murnane second for a radically inward, formally consistent fiction that is thematically narrow by design. He also treats Michon's compact oeuvre as a limit on the weight of the corpus, while crediting its stylistic intensity.
responses.response: I agree that the Cărtărescu case should be made for the whole body of work, and that is how I have framed the citation. On Murnane, I did not rank him, and I take the point that his integrity and consistency are real. The narrowness he accepts by design is the very feature that makes me hesitate over the 'significance across the body of work' criterion. Michon is a different case, because there the prose is as exacting as any on the shortlist, but I share the worry that translation carries little of it and that the oeuvre is slim. For both writers I would want their breadth of significance argued, not assumed.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's language-level achievement, including Romanian rhythm and syntax, survives in the English and French translations on which most readers' judgment relies.
Whether the length and digressive density of the late novels is sustained purposeful pattern or partial overextension; this needs close reading of the whole corpus.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's early poetry and short prose in translation is thin, so my view of the full oeuvre is partial.
For Carson, how far book-objects, translations and occasional pieces should count toward a literary citation, and how her hybrid work relates to the Nobel will's wording on 'idealistic tendency'.
My assessments rely on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions; I have not independently verified any sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile that would require recusal. My scholarly interests in the literary fragment, exile literature and the translation of Celan overlap thematically with some candidates' concerns, notably Carson's use of fragment and translation, but the profile documents no personal or professional relationship with any shortlisted writer. A member's own literary practice is context, not evidence of preference.
